name: Muscles of the trunk (abdominal wall and back)
description: Anterior abdominal wall, posterior abdominal wall, breathing and deep back muscles (right side), with the axial skeleton for context.

source.attribution: BodyParts3D, (c) The Database Center for Life Science, licensed under CC Attribution-Share Alike 2.1 Japan
source.anatomy_verified: Geometry and identity taken from BodyParts3D (FMA IDs preserved). Shapes simplified for the web only.
source.conversion_notes: Binary STL converted to GLB: vertices welded, meshes simplified with quadric decimation for web delivery, smooth normals, axes converted to Y-up/Z-anterior, recentred, one node per structure. Structures marked "merged" are the union of several BodyParts3D meshes (e.g. the parts of one muscle); structures with a "component" take one connected part of a BodyParts3D mesh, chosen by position.

groups.label: Muscles of the trunk
groups.tip: Think in layers: flat belly muscles in front, a deep back wall and pelvic floor, and long columns up your back. Front muscles bend you forward, back muscles straighten you.

groups.label: Skeleton (context)
groups.tip: Most trunk muscles stretch between your ribs, spine and pelvis. Find the bony points first, then the muscle between them.

groups.label: Anterolateral abdominal wall
groups.tip: Three flat muscles, outside in: external oblique like hands in your pockets, internal oblique across it, and transversus like a corset. Rectus abdominis runs straight down the front.

groups.label: Posterior abdominal wall and pelvic floor
groups.tip: C three, four, five keeps the diaphragm alive. Psoas and quadratus lumborum lie side by side at the back of the belly, and levator ani forms the pelvic floor below.

groups.label: Back muscles
groups.tip: The back columns, outside in, are I Love Spaghetti: iliocostalis, longissimus, spinalis. Deeper still, multifidus and semispinalis tie the vertebrae together like short straps.

groups.label: Neck muscles
groups.tip: Sternocleidomastoid turns your face to the opposite side, while splenius turns it to the same side. The scalenes lift your top two ribs.

synonyms: Vertebral column, ribs, sternum and pelvis

content.origin: Axial comes from axis, the central line of the body. Skeleton comes from a Greek word meaning dried up.
content.location: The bony core of your trunk: the spine, ribs, breastbone and pelvis. It is shown here so you can see where the muscles attach.
content.description: A frame of bones that the trunk muscles hold on to, from the ribs and spine down to the hip bones, sacrum and tailbone.
content.function: It holds you upright and guards your heart, lungs, belly organs and spinal cord. It also gives the belly and back muscles something to pull on.
content.mnemonic: Axial means along the axis. Think of the skull, spine, ribs and breastbone as the pole down the middle of you.
content.clinical: Fragile bones in osteoporosis can make vertebrae collapse. People may lose height and develop a forward stoop.
content.hint: The bony frame behind and around all the trunk muscles.

content.origin: From the Latin rectus, meaning straight. It is the straight muscle of the belly.
content.location: A long strap down the front of your belly, one on each side of the middle line. It runs from the pubic bone up to the lower ribs, inside a sheath.
content.description: Long and flat, wider at the top. Bands of tendon cross it, splitting it into the blocks you see as a six-pack in lean people.
content.function: It curls your trunk forward, like in a sit-up or crunch. It also squeezes your belly and helps tip your pelvis back.
content.mnemonic: Rectus runs right up the middle, a straight muscle for a straight crunch.
content.clinical: In pregnancy, the two straps can drift apart along the middle line. This is called diastasis recti and can leave a bulge down the belly.
content.hint: The straight, segmented strap on either side of the middle at the front of the belly, from pubic bone to lower ribs.

questions.text: What is the main action of the rectus abdominis?
questions.explanation: The rectus abdominis curls your trunk forward, just like in a sit-up.

questions.text: What splits the rectus abdominis into its six-pack blocks?
questions.explanation: Bands of tendon, called tendinous intersections, cross the muscle and make the six-pack blocks.

content.origin: From the Latin words for slanting and outer. It is the outer slanting muscle.
content.location: The outermost and biggest of the three flat muscles on the side of your belly. It wraps from the lower ribs around to the front.
content.description: A wide, thin sheet with fibres running down and in, like hands in your front pockets. Its lower edge rolls under to make the inguinal ligament in the groin.
content.function: It squeezes your belly and bends your trunk. The right one twists your trunk to the left, and it also bends you to the right.
content.mnemonic: External oblique fibres run like hands in your front pockets, down and in.
content.clinical: Its flat tendon has an opening near the groin, the outer end of the inguinal canal. An inguinal hernia can bulge out through it.
content.hint: The outermost flat sheet on the side of the belly, with fibres slanting down and in like hands in front pockets.

questions.text: The right external oblique twists the trunk toward which side?
options: It does not twist the trunk
Only when the arm is raised
questions.explanation: The external oblique twists your trunk toward the opposite side, so the right one turns you left.

questions.text: Which ligament is made by the lower edge of the external oblique?
questions.explanation: Its flat tendon folds under at the bottom to form the inguinal ligament in your groin.

content.origin: From the Latin words for slanting and inner. It is the inner slanting muscle.
content.location: The middle of the three flat muscles on the side of your belly. It lies under the external oblique and on top of the transversus abdominis.
content.description: A thin sheet whose fibres fan up and in, crossing the outer layer at right angles. In males, some of its lowest fibres carry on around the cord to the testis.
content.function: It squeezes your belly and bends your trunk. It twists and bends you toward its own side.
content.mnemonic: Internal oblique is the opposite of external. Its fibres run up and in, like hands resting on your lower ribs.
content.clinical: Its lowest fibres form the cremaster muscle. Stroking the inner thigh makes the testis lift, a reflex doctors sometimes test.
content.hint: The middle flat layer on the side of the belly, with fibres fanning up and in at right angles to the outer layer.

questions.text: Where does the internal oblique lie?
options: On top of the external oblique
Between the external oblique and transversus
questions.explanation: The internal oblique is the middle layer, sandwiched between the other two flat belly muscles.

content.origin: From the Latin transversus, meaning lying across. Its fibres run across your belly.
content.location: The deepest of the three flat muscles on the side of your belly, under the internal oblique. It wraps around from your back to the front.
content.description: A thin sheet with fibres running mostly side to side, like a corset or a weightlifting belt.
content.function: It pulls your belly in tight and steadies your trunk and lower back. Draw your belly button in toward your spine and you are using it.
content.mnemonic: Transversus means fibres going across. It is your body's own corset.
content.clinical: The nerves of the belly wall run between this muscle and the internal oblique. Doctors inject numbing medicine there, a TAP block, to ease pain after surgery.
content.hint: The deepest flat layer on the side of the belly, with side-to-side fibres that wrap it like a corset.

questions.text: Which belly muscle has side-to-side fibres and works like a corset?
questions.explanation: The transversus abdominis wraps around your belly with across-running fibres and pulls it in like a corset.

content.origin: From the Latin word for pyramid-shaped. It is a small triangle of muscle.
content.location: At the very bottom of the front of your belly, just above the pubic bone. It sits in front of the lower rectus abdominis.
content.description: A small triangle, wide at its base on the pubic bone and narrowing to a point on the middle line. Many people do not have one on one or both sides.
content.function: It tightens the linea alba, the tough white line of tendon running down the middle of your belly.
content.mnemonic: Pyramidalis is a tiny pyramid sitting on the pubic bone.
content.clinical: It is often missing, and nobody notices. Its job is so small that its absence causes no weakness of the belly wall.
content.hint: A tiny triangle at the lowest part of the front belly wall, sitting on the pubic bone in front of the segmented strap.

questions.text: What does the pyramidalis do?
questions.explanation: The pyramidalis pulls tight on the linea alba, the white line of tendon down the middle of your belly.

content.origin: From the Latin words for square and of the loins. It is the square muscle of the lower back.
content.location: Deep in the back wall of your belly, filling the gap between the twelfth rib and the top of the hip bone, beside the lower spine.
content.description: A flat, roughly square block of muscle between your lowest rib and the top of your pelvis.
content.function: It bends your trunk to its own side and helps arch your lower back. It can hitch one hip up and holds the twelfth rib steady when you breathe.
content.mnemonic: Quadratus means square. Picture a square block between your last rib and your hip bone.
content.clinical: Tightness or spasm here is a common part of low back pain. Massage therapists and physiotherapists often work on it.
content.hint: A flat square muscle filling the gap between the lowest rib and the top of the hip bone, beside the lower spine.

questions.text: Between which two bony landmarks does the quadratus lumborum lie?
questions.explanation: The quadratus lumborum fills the gap between your twelfth rib and the top of your hip bone, the iliac crest.

questions.text: What movement happens when one quadratus lumborum contracts?
options: Bending the trunk to the same side
questions.explanation: One side on its own pulls your trunk over sideways toward that side.

content.origin: From the Greek word for the loin muscles. Major means larger, because a small psoas minor is sometimes present.
content.location: Deep in the back of your belly, running down beside the lower spine. It crosses the rim of the pelvis and passes under the groin to reach the thigh.
content.description: A long, thick muscle, fat in the middle like a spindle. It joins the iliacus to form the iliopsoas, and a network of lower back nerves forms inside it.
content.function: It is the strongest muscle for lifting your thigh forward at the hip. It pulls on the lesser trochanter, a bump near the top of the thigh bone.
content.mnemonic: Psoas links your spine to your thigh, so as to lift your knee.
content.clinical: In appendicitis, stretching the right hip back can pull on the swollen area over the psoas and cause pain. Doctors call this the psoas sign.
content.hint: A long, thick muscle beside the lower spine that runs down over the rim of the pelvis to the thigh.

questions.text: What is the main action of the psoas major?
options: Lifting the thigh at the hip
questions.explanation: Together with the iliacus, the psoas major is the strongest muscle for bending the hip.

questions.text: Where does the psoas major attach on the thigh bone?
questions.explanation: The psoas major joins the iliacus and grips the lesser trochanter, a small bump near the top of the femur.

content.origin: From the Greek word for a partition or fence. It is the wall between your chest and your belly.
content.location: A dome between your chest and belly, fixed around the bottom of the rib cage and to the upper lower-back bones. The right dome sits higher, pushed up by the liver.
content.description: Muscle fibres run in from the edges to a flat central tendon, like a parachute. It has openings for the big vein, the food pipe and the aorta.
content.function: It is your main breathing muscle. As it tightens, the dome flattens, the chest gets taller and air rushes in.
content.mnemonic: C3, 4, 5 keeps the diaphragm alive, that is its phrenic nerve. For the openings, I 8 10 Eggs At 12: vena cava T8, oesophagus T10, aorta T12.
content.clinical: In a hiatus hernia, part of the stomach slides up through the food pipe opening. An irritated diaphragm can cause pain in the shoulder tip, because its nerve comes from C3 to C5.
content.hint: A dome-shaped sheet of muscle and tendon forming the floor of the chest and the roof of the belly.

questions.text: Which nerve supplies the diaphragm?
questions.explanation: The phrenic nerves, from C3, C4 and C5, drive the diaphragm. C3, 4, 5 keeps the diaphragm alive.

questions.text: At what level does the oesophagus pass through the diaphragm?
questions.explanation: The food pipe goes through at T10. The big vein goes through at T8 and the aorta at T12.

content.origin: From the Latin words for lifter and of the anus. It is the muscle that lifts the anus.
content.location: Across the bottom of your pelvis, from the pubic bone in front to the tailbone behind. With the small coccygeus it forms the pelvic floor.
content.description: A wide, thin sheet like a hammock, made of three parts shown together. The front part forms a U-shaped sling around the back of the rectum.
content.function: It holds up your pelvic organs and braces against pressure when you cough or lift. Its sling keeps a bend in the bowel that helps you stay continent.
content.mnemonic: Levator ani is the pelvic hammock. Its parts from front to back are puborectalis, pubococcygeus and iliococcygeus, so P, P, I.
content.clinical: Stretching or damage in childbirth can weaken it, leading to leaks of urine or sagging pelvic organs. Pelvic floor exercises help make it stronger.
content.hint: The muscular hammock forming the floor of the pelvis, between the pubic bone in front and the tailbone behind.

questions.text: Which of these is NOT a part of the levator ani?
questions.explanation: The levator ani has three parts, puborectalis, pubococcygeus and iliococcygeus. Iliocostalis is a back muscle.

questions.text: What is a common cause of weakness in the levator ani?
questions.explanation: Stretching or injury during childbirth can weaken the pelvic floor.

content.origin: From the Latin words for the hip bone and a rib. It runs from the hip bone up to the ribs.
content.location: The outer column of the three long muscles that run up either side of your spine. It climbs over the bends of the ribs, beside the longissimus.
content.description: Shown here as one muscle with three parts, for the lower back, chest and neck. Each part climbs a few levels and grips higher up.
content.function: Both sides together straighten and arch your spine. One side alone bends your spine toward that side.
content.mnemonic: The back columns from outside in are I Love Spaghetti, iliocostalis, longissimus, spinalis. Iliocostalis is outermost and goes to the ribs.
content.clinical: Like the other long back muscles, it is often strained when you lift with a bent back. This causes low back pain and spasm.
content.hint: The outermost of the three upright columns of back muscles, attaching to the bends of the ribs.

questions.text: Which column of the erector spinae is furthest out to the side?
questions.explanation: From outside in, the columns are iliocostalis, longissimus and spinalis. Remember I Love Spaghetti.

questions.text: What happens when both iliocostalis muscles contract together?
options: The spine straightens and arches back
The head turns to the opposite side
questions.explanation: Working together, the long back columns straighten your spine and arch it backward.

content.origin: From the Latin word for the longest. It is the longest of the back muscles.
content.location: The middle column of the three long back muscles, between the iliocostalis and the spinalis. It runs from the sacrum all the way up to the skull.
content.description: Shown here as one muscle with three parts. The chest part is the biggest, and the top part reaches the bump behind your ear.
content.function: Both sides together straighten your spine and tip your head back. One side alone bends your spine and turns your head toward that side.
content.mnemonic: In I Love Spaghetti, L is for Longissimus, the long one in the middle.
content.clinical: It is the thickest of the long back muscles in the lower back. That is where most back strains are felt.
content.hint: The middle and longest of the three upright back columns, reaching from the sacrum up to the bump behind the ear.

questions.text: The top part of longissimus attaches to which part of the skull?
questions.explanation: Longissimus capitis grips the mastoid process, the bump you can feel behind your ear.

content.origin: From the Latin word spina, meaning a thorn or the spine. It runs between the pointed spines of the vertebrae.
content.location: The innermost and smallest of the three long back columns. It lies right beside the bony bumps down the middle of your back, mostly in the chest region.
content.description: Shown here as one muscle with a chest part and a neck part. It links the spine of one vertebra to the spines of others above.
content.function: Both sides together straighten your spine. One side alone bends it toward that side.
content.mnemonic: In I Love Spaghetti, Spinalis is the one closest to the Spine.
content.clinical: It is small and close to the middle, so it is rarely hurt on its own. It does tighten up with the other back muscles in back spasm.
content.hint: The innermost and smallest upright back column, linking the bony bumps right beside the middle line.

questions.text: What does the spinalis attach to?
questions.explanation: Spinalis runs from one spinous process to another, the bony bumps down the middle of your back.

content.origin: From the Latin words for many and to split. It is split into many small parts.
content.location: Deep in your back, in the groove right beside the bony bumps of the spine, under the long back muscles. It is thickest in the lower back.
content.description: Lots of short bundles, each crossing two to four vertebrae. They run up and in from a lower anchor to the spine of a vertebra above.
content.function: It holds each vertebra steady as you move, like guy ropes on a tent pole. It also helps straighten, side-bend and twist the spine.
content.mnemonic: Multifidus means many fingers. Many small bundles each grip a spine a few levels up.
content.clinical: In people with long-lasting low back pain, the lower part is often weak or shrunken. So it is a key target of core stability exercises.
content.hint: Many short deep bundles in the groove next to the spine, thickest in the lower back beneath the long back columns.

questions.text: What is a key job of the multifidus?
options: Holding the vertebrae steady during movement
Lifting the thigh at the hip
questions.explanation: Multifidus holds each vertebra steady and helps straighten and twist the spine.

content.origin: From the Latin words for half and of the spine. It only covers the upper half of the spine.
content.location: Deep in your upper back and neck, under the splenius and trapezius and on top of the multifidus.
content.description: Shown here as one muscle with three parts. The top part is the biggest, forming the thick rope on each side of the middle at the back of your neck.
content.function: It tips your head back and straightens your neck and upper back. One side alone twists the spine toward the other side.
content.mnemonic: Semispinalis covers half the spine, only the neck and chest half.
content.clinical: The greater occipital nerve pierces its top part. Tension here is linked to headaches at the back of the head.
content.hint: The thick deep ropes on each side of the middle at the back of the neck, running up to the base of the skull.

questions.text: Which nerve pierces semispinalis capitis and may cause headaches at the back of the head?
questions.explanation: The greater occipital nerve passes through semispinalis capitis. Squeezing it here can cause headaches at the back of the head.

questions.text: In which part of the spine is the semispinalis found?
options: The upper half, neck and chest
The whole spine from sacrum to skull
questions.explanation: Semi means half. Semispinalis covers only the upper half of the spine, in the neck and chest.

content.origin: From the Latin words for saw-toothed, at the back and upper. It is the upper saw-toothed muscle at the back.
content.location: In your upper back, under the rhomboids. It runs from the bottom of the neck and top of the chest spine out to the upper ribs.
content.description: A thin, four-sided sheet with saw-tooth fingers that grip the ribs.
content.function: It is said to lift ribs two to four and help you breathe in. It may work more as a sensor that tracks rib position than as a strong mover.
content.mnemonic: The superior one pulls the upper ribs up. The inferior one pulls the lower ribs down.
content.clinical: It sits under the rhomboids and shoulder blade. Massage therapists sometimes see it as a source of pain around the shoulder blade.
content.hint: A thin saw-toothed sheet in the upper back, running from the lower neck spines to ribs two to four under the shoulder blade muscles.

questions.text: What action is usually given for serratus posterior superior?
options: Turns the head to the same side
questions.explanation: Serratus posterior superior is said to lift ribs two to four, helping you breathe in.

content.origin: From the Latin words for saw-toothed, at the back and lower. It is the lower saw-toothed muscle at the back.
content.location: In your lower back, under the latissimus dorsi. It runs from the spine around T11 to L2 out to the lowest ribs.
content.description: A thin, four-sided sheet whose fingers run up and out to grip ribs eight to twelve.
content.function: It is said to pull the lower ribs down and back. It may work more as a sensor that tracks rib position than as a strong mover.
content.mnemonic: Inferior means lower. The inferior serratus pulls the lower ribs down.
content.clinical: It lies under the latissimus dorsi and can be strained with it. This gives pain over the lower ribs at the back.
content.hint: A thin saw-toothed sheet in the lower back, running from the lower chest and upper lumbar spines to the lowest ribs.

questions.text: Serratus posterior inferior attaches to which ribs?
questions.explanation: Serratus posterior inferior grips the lowest five ribs, eight to twelve.

names.latin: Musculi splenius capitis et splenius cervicis

content.origin: From a Greek word for a bandage. It wraps around the deeper neck muscles like a bandage.
content.location: At the back of your neck and upper back, under the trapezius. It covers the deeper neck muscles, such as semispinalis.
content.description: Shown here as one muscle with a head part and a neck part. Its fibres run up and out like a wrapped bandage, reaching the bump behind the ear.
content.function: Both sides together tip your head and neck back. One side alone bends your neck and turns your head toward that same side.
content.mnemonic: Splenius is a splint or bandage wrapped around the back of your neck.
content.clinical: It is often strained in whiplash, when the head snaps back and forth in a car crash. This causes neck pain and stiffness.
content.hint: A bandage-like sheet wrapping up and out over the deep muscles at the back of the neck, reaching the bump behind the ear.

questions.text: When one splenius contracts, it turns the head toward which side?
questions.explanation: One splenius turns your head toward its own side.

questions.text: The name splenius comes from a word meaning what?
questions.explanation: Splenius comes from the Greek for a bandage, because it wraps around the neck.

content.origin: Named after where it attaches: the sternum or breastbone, the clavicle or collarbone, and the mastoid bump behind the ear.
content.location: On the side of your neck, running on a slant from the top of the breastbone and collarbone up to the bump behind your ear.
content.description: A thick strap with two heads at the bottom, one on the breastbone and one on the collarbone. They join into one belly running up and back.
content.function: One side tilts your head to its own side and turns your face the other way. Both together bend your neck forward. The accessory nerve drives it.
content.mnemonic: To turn your face to the left, you use your right one. Your face looks away from the muscle that is working.
content.clinical: In wry neck, or torticollis, a shortened muscle keeps the head tilted and turned. Babies can be born with a firm lump in it that causes this.
content.hint: The big slanting strap on the side of the neck, from the top of the breastbone and collarbone to the bump behind the ear.

questions.text: The right sternocleidomastoid turns the face toward which side?
options: It does not turn the head
questions.explanation: Each sternocleidomastoid turns your face to the opposite side, so the right one turns it left.

questions.text: Which nerve makes the sternocleidomastoid move?
questions.explanation: The accessory nerve, cranial nerve eleven, drives this muscle.

content.origin: From the Greek word for uneven, like a scalene triangle with sides of different lengths.
content.location: Deep on the side of your neck, behind the sternocleidomastoid. They run from the neck bones down to the first two ribs.
content.description: Shown here as one muscle with three parts. The front and middle parts reach the first rib, and the back part reaches the second rib.
content.function: They lift the first and second ribs when you breathe in hard, like after a sprint. They also bend your neck to the side.
content.mnemonic: Front and middle go to rib one, back goes to rib two. The arm nerves squeeze through between the front and middle ones.
content.clinical: The arm nerves and main arm artery pass between the front and middle scalenes. If they get squeezed here, the arm can ache, tingle or feel weak.
content.hint: Three deep bands on the side of the neck, behind the big slanting strap, running from the neck bones down to the first two ribs.

questions.text: What passes between the front and middle scalene muscles?
options: The brachial plexus and subclavian artery
The phrenic and vagus nerves only
The carotid artery and jugular vein
questions.explanation: The brachial plexus, the nerves to your arm, and the subclavian artery slip through the gap between these two muscles.

questions.text: What do the scalenes do when you breathe?
options: Lift ribs one and two when you breathe in hard
questions.explanation: The scalenes lift the first two ribs to help you take a big, deep breath.
